speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF NEW COMMANDER IN CHIEF
speechtext: With the leave of the house, Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the President of the United States, with the concurrence of the Canadian government, has appointed General Laurence S. Kuter to replace General Earle E. Partridge as commander in chief, North American air defence command, effective upon the retirement of General Partridge on July 31, General Partridge having reached by that date the statutory age limit for his rank. Air Marshal C. R. Slemon, of the Royal Canadian Air Force, will continue in the appointment of deputy commander, North American air defence command. An announcement of this change of command is being made at this time in Washington.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF NEW COMMANDER IN CHIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all of us in this house are sorry to learn of General Partridge's retirement. He has been indeed a very great strength to NORAD. He is an outstanding airman and an outstanding public servant. We all wish him well in his retirement. I think at the same time, Mr. Speaker, we would like to pay tribute to Air Marshal Slemon, the deputy commander, for the long and excellent service he has given to this country and for the continued contribution he is making in this position. He is an airman's airman, and an officer of whom this country can be proud.
The airmen under NORAD are carrying on an important task under very difficult circumstances, and to them we owe our support and our appreciation. We congratulate the new commander upon his appointment. We wish him every success in this new, very difficult and demanding role. We hope the government of Canada will give him every possible support in the carrying out of his responsibilities and we would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that they pay greater attention to his advice than they have paid to that of the retiring chief.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF NEW COMMANDER IN CHIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have all noted with interest the statement by the Minister of National
Defence relative to the retirement of the United States commander of NORAD, and the information that a Canadian still holds the position of second in command. We also wish the retiring commander a very long, happy and pleasurable retirement.
In view of the fact that the change in command, as illustrated by the statement of the Minister of National Defence, is strictly because General Partridge has now reached the retirement age in the rank he holds, we certainly hope that a full discussion in this House of Commons will be allowed, perhaps led by the Minister of National Defence, of the entire issue of NORAD because of the fact that both the retiring commander of NORAD and the Canadian who is second in command have both publicly questioned the position or the status, the responsibility and the methods of air defence of North America. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion No. 100-Mr. Argue:
For a copy of any letter or letters exchanged since January 1, 1958 between the Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland and the minister of municipal affairs of Newfoundland, regarding the appointment of federal nominees to the St, John's housing authority.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ST. JOHN'S HOUSING AUTHORITY  FEDERAL NOMINEES
speechtext:
If the house will permit me, I would like to say something about this notice of motion. In view of the discussion which has taken place earlier about questions to and returns by ministers without portfolio, may I say that normally a motion for production of papers is directed to a minister who has responsibility for a department, and in this case, as the subject matter appears to be a housing authority, I assume it would be the Minister of Public Works. And so I asked myself whether in the circumstances any part of this motion could be within the

competence of the house and in accord with the practice in respect to the production of papers.
I considered the matter in consultation with the Clerk of the house. I could not say definitely that the notice of motion was necessarily beyond the competence of the house in all respects, and in the circumstances I felt that I should not deprive the house of the opportunity of deciding for itself whether or not it could call for the production of these papers after I had indicated to the house the considerations which had prompted me to raise the question.
Briefly they are as follows. There are two cases where the house calls for the production of documents. One is for public papers from a department of government, and the other is for communications made by the government as a whole. In this particular case the minister named in the motion has no department of government and is therefore excluded from the responsibility of producing documents from a department. On the other hand he is a privy councillor, a minister of the crown and a member of the government, and therefore in respect of acts in his official capacity as a member of the government he is presumably amenable to the jurisdiction of the house with regard to the production of documents, subject to the limitations of public policy and so on, which pass through him in that capacity.
I therefore came to the conclusion that the order, if it were issued, would have to be read as though it limited itself to communications made on behalf of the government. In other words it would have to be considered as reading this way:
-for a copy of any letter or letters exchanged since January 1, 1958, between the Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland on behalf of the government and the minister of municipal affairs of Newfoundland regarding the appointment of federal nominees to the St. John's housing authority.
It would be possible to put the question as it stands with that necessary qualification being understood, but I think it would be better if I directed that the motion be amended by inserting those words before it is put to the house, as I have authority to do in accordance with the precedents as cited in Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 199.
Before making any move, however, since this is a matter of some interest, I would be happy to hear, within reason, what any hon. members wish to say. May I first give you the authorities for the views I have expressed. May, in his sixteenth edition, at page 273, indicates:
(a)	that returns may be moved relating to any public matter in which the house or the crown has jurisdiction;

(b)	that these documents may be obtained from all public offices and from corporations, bodies, or offices constituted for public purposes, by acts of parliament or otherwise; and
(c)	that the papers and correspondence sought from government departments should be of a public and official character and not private or confidential.
Campion, to the same effect, in his Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons, third edition, says:
Returns are of two kinds, either to an order of the house, or to an address to the crown. This distinction, which corresponds to the constitutional origin of the departments, is still rigorously observed. It amounts to this-that information which is wanted from a department which originally grew out of the royal prerogative, such as a department of a secretary of state, is prayed for by an humble address to the crown, whereas information required from a financial department or from a department constituted under statute is demanded by an order of the house.
There is one further reference. In his book Parliament, Its History, Constitution and Practice, Sir Courtenay Ilbert, former clerk of the British house of commons, explains at page 114 that the asking of questions is not the only mode by which the house can obtain information from or through the government, and he then adds:
It can, on the motion of any member, obtain returns supplying such information on matters of public importance as is obtainable through departments of the government.
I might also point out that Beauchesne in his fourth edition under citation 209 has something to say on the subject. What I proposed to suggest to the house was to insert those words and allow the house to decide whether these documents should be produced.

subtopic: ST. JOHN'S HOUSING AUTHORITY  FEDERAL NOMINEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the insertion of the words "on behalf of the government" is concerned I would suggest that in essence this really should not restrict the motion, because the letters in question that have been referred to publicly were written to a minister of the crown of the province of Newfoundland. Since they were written by a federal cabinet minister to a provincial cabinet minister about federal appointees to a housing authority, the housing authority itself having been the subject of an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland, I would say this is definitely a public matter and this is an official communication and therefore should be produced.
You have said that motions such as this are ordinarily directed to the minister who has authority over the department concerned. I would point out to Your Honour that there have been a number of motions passed in this house on previous occasions when we have had ministers without portfolio. The
Motion for Papers
motions have been passed in general terms and I would suggest in such terms as to make it necessary to divulge the kind of correspondence to which this motion is directed.
I would refer Your Honour to a motion moved on May 11, 1931, when in fact there were ministers without portfolio. It reads:
A copy of all petitions, resolutions, recommendations, letters, telegrams, documents, reports, as well as an epitome of all verbal representations addressed or communicated to the prime minister, the minister of agriculture, or any other minister, recommending the pegging of wheat or grain prices from any farmers' organizations, pool selling agency or unit thereof, municipality, board of trade, service club, community association and individual or collection of individuals, from the North Battleford federal constituency since July 28 last, and the respective replies thereto.
A second motion of a similar character was moved and passed on July 20, 1931, and reads as follows:
A copy of all letters, telegrams and representations made by any person, party or organization in Canada to any minister of the crown in connection with the duty on potatoes coming into Canada and their valuation for duty purposes; also a copy of all orders in council passed in connection with same, since August, 1930.
In the return that was produced each minister, including ministers without portfolio, had been canvassed as to whether or not they had any correspondence in this field.

A copy of all correspondence exchanged since June 21, 1957, between any member of the provincial governments and any member of the federal government concerning the federal-provincial taxsharing agreements.
I would submit that since these motions have been moved and passed, and since a cabinet minister is a member of the government-I do not think there is any question about that-this motion is proper. Even if

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. I wonder if his department is considering any changes to the Welland ship canal section of the seaway which, according to today's Globe and Mail, is causing a major traffic jam?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL  REPORTED TRAFFIC JAM

Mr. Speaker, the heavy concentration of upbound shipping off Port Weller, where some 37 vessels are waiting to enter the Welland ship canal, is largely the result of the unusual number of ships on hand for the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speechtext:
I move:
That clause 5 of BUI C-32, an act to amend the War Service Grants Act, be amended by adding thereto, after line 5 on page 3, the following provision:
"9B. Notwithstanding anything in this act, where a member of the forces who is unmarried has, because of a mental infirmity that confined him to hospital, been unable to use all the re-establishment credit for which he is eligible under this act before the expiration of the period within which that credit may be made available to him, the minister may, on application by that member within one year of the date of his discharge from hospital, make available to him any unused portion of his re-establishment credit."

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, RE-ESTABLISHMENT CREDITS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am very pleased to see this amendment, as I was checking through the bill just prior to the minister making the announcement that he intended to introduce it. This was one question which was pretty thoroughly discussed in the committee, as the result of representations made by Mr. Thompson, in particular, of the Canadian Legion. I judge from reading the amendment now that it does meet the fears expressed by Mr. Thompson on behalf of the Legion and expressed by members of all parties in the committee when they were discussing the representations made by Mr. Thompson. I would like to say we are very happy to support this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, RE-ESTABLISHMENT CREDITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this clause may I just make this remark. As the hon. member has just stated, this point was brought up in the committee by a representative of the Legion, and more particularly by some of our own members on the committee especially the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Speakman). It is a point that was very well taken and it shows the great value of having a veterans committee studying veterans legislation. The purpose of the clause as it reads is to extend the availability of re-establishment credit to the dependants

War Service Grants Act of those veterans who are mentally infirm. It enables the credit to be used for the benefit of the veteran's household on application to the minister within one year of the date of his discharge from hospital, and he would be entitled to any unused portion of his credit. The act at present makes no provision for such contingencies.
The recommendation made by the committee was to the effect that a single veteran mentally infirm should not be deprived of his re-establishment credit, and then suggested that when his condition had improved to the extent that he could manage his affairs and such improvement had not taken place until the expiration of the normal time limit during which he was able to use that credit, such veteran should have a period of one year within which to use his credit. There would admittedly not be very many cases to which this clause would apply. I am very pleased indeed to get this recommendation from the committee, and we are very pleased to make this amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, RE-ESTABLISHMENT CREDITS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at the meeting of the committee this matter was decided by the committee. As a matter of fact the resolution was drawn up by one of the members, and I think some credit should be given to him. This matter has been reviewed on many occasions and discussed for the last five or six years, and finally we have resolved it into a piece of legislation today which is entirely satisfactory, I would suggest, to every veteran in the country.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the heart-rending appeal which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made in concluding his observations, it seems to me that there is not only a great deal to say but that there is need for much to be said about this bill.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
It may be recalled that a bill similar in all respects was introduced into this parliament a year ago, and also into the previous parliament a little more than a year ago. This is the third round of the same old thing. It seems to me that this business of bringing in this measure for one year at a time and holding out a kind of carrot to the provinces indicating that something is going to be done on some future occasion is a most inefficient way of using the time of parliament and of carrying on the affairs of this country.
When my friend, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) spoke during our discussion of this matter on the resolution stage, he described this as the annual reprieve of the government from its pre-election promises, and I suggested, speaking after him, that the government would continue to proceed in this way from year to year until at least 1962 which seems, if I may make a brief allusion to the bill which we were discussing just before this one, to be the final cut-off date favoured by this government.
Now the minister indicates that the government has no authority to pay this money. It seems to me that there is no need whatever for this situation to have arisen. The minister well knew, when he brought a similar bill before the house in the previous session that this government had no intention whatsoever of making any different provision this year, and there is no reason on earth why the bill of last year should not have applied for two years, or three years, or four years.
This government has not the faintest intention of doing anything more for the provinces at all. Hon. members of this government simply are not willing to get up and say so, however. That is what I said last August in the debate on the previous bill. I said that at most the provinces might receive telegrams but probably this year they would not even receive telegrams; the matter would be just presented to this house and that would be all there would be to it. I also said it would be done at the last possible moment in an endeavour to make a squeeze play-I did not use that phrase, but that is what it amounts to-on the House of Commons.
This is no way to treat parliament. This government that was going to be so respectful of parliament is simply using up the time of parliament in making these annual appropriations in exactly the same form when it knows perfectly well it does not intend to do anything different although, as I suggested the other day, there will probably be a deathbed repentance just before the next election

Dominion-Provincial Relations which I have no doubt is already being planned. I hope hon. members opposite will mark those words because like previous predictions that have been made in this field, I think my words will be borne out by the facts as they will unfold.
There is another thing that needs to be said about this particular bill. This bill is an amendment to the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act. It is an enactment of a new scheme for federal-provincial taxsharing that was devised very largely by the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, and the former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, with the very competent assistance of the able officers of the Department of Finance and other relevant branches of the public service. It was a vast improvement in two respects on any previous arrangements there had been in this field. It was an improvement financially in that, in the good times which we had three years ago, the federal government of that day showed a disposition to share the tax advantages to a much larger extent with the provinces than the present government has been willing to do.
In the second place, it was a much better arrangement because it did remove the last vestige of anything that could conceivably be described as a disability upon provinces which did not want to impose their taxes in exactly the same way as the federal taxes were imposed. In other words, if there was any suggestion-and I never thought there was much to it-that the old tax rental system in any way limited provincial autonomy, the new tax-sharing arrangement removed that suggestion. That is no doubt the reason why the premier of Quebec is now taking the money, which, of course, he did not do under the old tax rental arrangement. It should not be forgotten that it is a very handsome sum, indeed, that he is taking nor should it be forgotten that the people of Quebec would be very much worse off as far as provincial services are concerned or as far as provincial taxation is concerned, or more likely both, if it had not been for the constructive and statesmanlike efforts of Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris and the present leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage-

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The minister, of course, is bringing in a bill one year at a time just for the sake of attempting to kid the troops, and I shall not proceed very long in my remarks before I shall be able to show that that is exactly why it is being done. This method is already wearing pretty thin.
Why do we not have a bill that will run for the same period of time as the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, until 1962? I will tell you why, sir, and I will tell the minister too although he knows it perfectly well. The reason we are not doing it is because there are provincial elections this year in Manitoba and Ontario. My hon. friends opposite, ably assisted by the party's chief of staff, are trying to win those elections by, among other things, giving the impression that something is going to be done about this in the very near future. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) attempted to elicit some information from the Minister of Finance on the orders of the day, with the usual success we have in these matters.
I have here a quotation from one of the leading newspapers in this province, a newspaper very dear to the heart of the Minister of Finance. I refer to the Toronto Star of the day before yesterday, May 4. That issue carried an article in which the newspaper quotes the manifesto of the premier of Ontario in these words:
In the manifesto, Premier Frost disclosed there would be a federal-provincial conference "within the next month or two"-
That was before he got the minister's letter. He was jumping the gun a little, apparently. I continue:
-to initiate a study of Canada's entire structure of taxation and the expenditure and debt trends of each level of government.
A direct quotation then follows in these words:
"There is no doubt," he went on, "that this intensive and dispassionate study-
I like that word "dispassionate" study. There was nothing very dispassionate about those tear-jerking speeches the premier of Ontario was making a couple of years ago when he was appearing on the same platform

with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and was saying, "That is the man who is going to give us $100 million." There was no dispassionate study at that time and apparently the $100 million is now being devoted to a dispassionate study. Certainly it is not in the provincial treasury.
Returning to the article, the premier then went on to say:
"There is no doubt-that this intensive and dispassionate study will produce far-reaching fiscal reforms best calculated to render effective the great principles of our Canadian constitution."
It is obvious from that kind of language that there is an election impending.
The Minister of Finance and the premier of Ontario are engaged in this joint enterprise of trying to fool the people of Ontario once more into thinking that something is really going to be done about this matter, but we know perfectly well that this study group the minister has organized is little more than a pale reflection of the kind of conferences which were promised before the last federal election. Oh, I know that the minister is going to get up and say that this promise was made in the election campaign prior to the last election campaign, and so it does not count any more. The minister might be interested in knowing, however, that there are many people in this country who take public men-or at least some public men-at their word.
As I am going to be saying a great deal about federal-provincial conferences and as I know how sensitive the Minister of Finance is on this subject, I think I might anticipate the objection I expect he will raise whenever he thinks that anything I am saying is somewhat effective, by recalling to Your Honour's mind the fact that we did have a debate on a very small aspect of this subject which began with a motion moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) on February 9. That motion read:
This house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations.
The words of the motion may be found at page 826 of Hansard of February 9. I can assure Your Honour that I am not going to argue that the federal government should call a federal-provincial conference at once. I understand the rules of the house and I know that the Tory majority in this house decided there should not be a federal-provincial conference at once even if Mr. Frost wants one and in spite of the fact that Mr. Roblin wants one, or pretends he does. The Tory majority in the house put a steam roller over that motion. They would not allow it to pass. Therefore it is a decision of the
Dominion-Provincial Relations house and I am not going to transgress the rules of the house.
But I do think that when the minister replies he should tell us when this conference is going to be held, and I do not mean this pale imitation conference of bureaucrats who cannot decide anything and who, of course, should not be allowed to decide anything; but when a real, proper conference of heads of government is going to be held, or whether the government has any kind of intention of holding one at all, which I do not think they have. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think there has been a complete change in the attitude of the government since they came into office.
In the last parliament we were told very authoritatively by the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) what the situation was. On October 18, 1957 he was asked a question by Mr. Breton, the then very distinguished member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, whom all of us in this house miss, at least all of us in this party, and who, I predict, will be back. I read from the English translation as found on page 129 of Hansard:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. Solicitor General a question? When sitting in the opposition the hon. Solicitor General has, on various occasions, given expression to the well-known thought that federal subsidies are unconstitutional. That was the one in November, the shadow meeting.
-could he tell us now if he would oppose the subsidies which his government seems to be preparing at this time?
Here is the answer by the Solicitor General:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell my hon. friend that I am still opposed to subsidies such as were proposed by the former government.
"I am still opposed." These subsidies so-called are still being paid. A slight increase has been made by the present government, but surely if a thing is wrong, to do a little more of it is even more wrong. Yet the Solicitor General, despite his capacity as a law officer, is now compounding this wrong. At that time, it was suggested by an hon. member that the question was a political one, and the Solicitor General went on:
And a political one, yes.
Since when has it become improper to ask political questions in a political assembly?
I want to tell him that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known-
How right he was! They are not yet known, and heaven knows when they will be known!
-but I am convinced-
Though nobody knew what they were.
-that they will be made on a very different basis from those of the former government.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Then we got, of course, a small instalment precisely on the scheme of the former government. The questioning was pursued but I will not take up the time of the committee to read all that intervened. It is very interesting and can be found on pages 129 and 130 if hon. members want to read it. But I intervened-perhaps it will not surprise some of the newer members to hear this-and addressed a question to the acting prime minister, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green). The question I asked him was this:
I ask the leader of the government, is there any intention whatsoever on the part of the federal government to substitute something else for the equalization grants?
This was the reply of the Minister of Public Works:
Well, now, Mr. Speaker-
We all know the way the Minister of Public Works speaks.
-I suggest that the hon. member for Twillingate-Bona vista-

speechtext:
Oh, Bonavista-Twillingate-he is all twisted up anyway.
That, I thought, was a remarkable contribution to the debate.
I suggest that he has already had his answer from the Solicitor General and he should know better than anybody else in this house that announcements of policy will be made in due course by the government.
We know that all announcements by this government are going to be made in due course, and "in due course" is coming to be more and more and more like eternity. The Solicitor General, having told us that on no account would this government continue payments to the provinces on the same basis as the Liberal government we had, of course, the events we all remember in January of 1958 when the Minister of Finance got his arithmetic all wrong and allowed all of the provinces to expect more than they got and some of them to expect more than, after a bad week end, even the Minister of Finance thought they were likely to get.
From that day until this, we have never had the faintest hint of what was in the mind of the government until the speech made by one hon. member from the province of Quebec who last Thursday was preaching for a call. The hon. gentleman, who made a very bright and intelligent speech, is already rumoured as likely to be, if not the next minister of finance, at least the parliamentary secretary to the next minister of finance. I am sure that considering the limitations on the choice of the government that choice would be welcomed in some quarters at any rate. The hon. gentleman had this to say, as found on page 3197 of Hansard of April 30:

(Translation):
When the central government convened the provincial representatives in 1957, it listened to their proposals, but soon realized that there were such differences of opinion between them that it became necessary to go very deeply into that problem.
(Text):
A very profound study would have to be made of this matter, a very profound study going on at least until 1962 and maybe beyond that. That is not what we were told before the election before the last. Before the election before the last, when the hon. gentlemen now occupying the treasury benches were going about the country preaching for a call, they had no doubt that they had the solution right up their sleeves.
(Translation):

speechtext: You said that last week.

speechtext:
I see that the Tremblay is trembling.
(Text):
They had the solution. The solution was all there. There was no problem at all. There was no profound study needed. All the people needed to do was to elect the Conservative party and this problem would be solved forthwith.
We all remember that touching scene in Toronto on April 25, 1957, when Mr. Frost and the Prime Minister appeared together on the same platform to open the campaign and Mr. Frost appealed to the people and said-it must have been very touching indeed-"Don't let them work you to death, John. We need you." They may have needed him, but they have not got much out of him. I could go on reading this sob story. I do not think the meeting was quite what was expected, because Mr. Frost spoke so long that the Prime Minister, according to the Canadian Press, had to cut three-quarters of his own speech and even then it went on until nearly midnight. But there were some things said on that occasion that I think are perhaps worth recalling today. For example, the Globe and Mail reported as follows:
Mr. Frost, whose appearance on the platform with Mr. Diefenbaker gave the rally a significant air of party solidarity, hit hard at the tax-sharing deal which the Liberal government offered the provinces ... "I say that the solution lies in a realistic division of tax sources in the direct tax field which belongs equally to the provinces and the federal government. It is not a matter of the federal government giving Ontario or the provinces anything. That is the patronizing attitude of Ottawa.
Now they do not even give!
All we ask is a reasonable part of our own, a part which is commensurate with the size of the job we have to do, and upon the accomplishment of which much of Canada's future depends."

Then, the present Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition, had this to say at that same meeting and I think the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) should listen to what his leader said on this occasion because it is very different from what has happened.
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation-
Imagine, sir, saying that after Mr. St. Laurent had been prime minister of this country for nine years and when there was a greater degree of unity than there had ever been before or than there has been at any time since.
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation; have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue;-
What amount extra have they got since?
-have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilities or permitting the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are. We believe the provinces and municipalities must have the financial resources to carry out those responsibilities. We believe in the federal system of government.
That, of course, is a remarkable assertion!
We believe in the federal system of government.
These are the people who send telegrams out to tell the provincial governments concerned what they are going to get.
We believe that its preservation is essential to Canadian unity. We believe the federal system is today being challenged by the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government and that a healthy division and balance of revenues as between the federal and provincial governments must be assured.
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.
That was the first speech in Toronto, and there were variations on this theme right across the country. Because there were some variations I intend, in order to be completely fair to hon. gentlemen opposite, which I always try to be, to give some of these variations. For example, I quote from the first television broadcast the Prime Minister delivered on April 30, 1957:
Since they came into power-
That is the Liberals.
-they have more than doubled the percentage of the federal portion of the taxation dollar. They have left the provinces and the municipalities fewer and fewer sources of revenues for their expanding requirements.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Since the minister's latest budget a higher proportion of the taxes of this country is being taken by the federal government than ever before in our history.
Then, at Hull, on May 7, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of May 8, we find the then leader of the opposition saying:
"One of the first steps to be taken by any government which I am called upon to lead", he said, "is to call a dominion-provincial conference to discuss a fair apportionment of sources of revenue as between the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities."
Well, the municipalities were forgotten along the way somewhere as we all know. Then, at Guelph, on May 13, as reported in the London Free Press of May 4, we find this:
Mr. Diefenbaker asserted that a Conservative government would convene this autumn a dominion-provincial conference to ensure that the provinces and the municipalities had a reasonable share of the tax dollar.
Then the present Prime Minister went into a province where there is, if I may say so without offence to the people of any other province, a more acute understanding of federal-provincial tax problems. This matter has been discussed for longer in that province than any other province. I refer to the province in which I spent 30 years of my life, Manitoba, because it was in that province under Mr. Bracken, Mr. Garson and latterly Mr. Campbell, that this problem of taxsharing was preached to the people. When the Prime Minister went to Winnipeg, therefore, there were some doubts in a good many people's minds, including apparently the Prime Minister's, about how some of this doctrine he was preaching was being received. There were some questions in many people's minds about whether the equalization system was going to be continued. The Prime Minister gave a press conference in Winnipeg which was reported in the Winnipeg Free Press. This is on May 14, 1957, and it reads:
Conservative Leader John Diefenbaker In Winnipeg today denied any claim that he was "buying" the support of Ontario Premier Leslie Frost with promises of a better federal-provincial tax agreement deal for Ontario which could work against the prairie provinces.
Such a suggestion, said Mr. Diefenbaker in an interview here, had "absolutely no foundation". There never had been any "direct or indirect suggestion" by Premier Frost that he would expect better tax terms from a Conservative government.
And he added that any person saying otherwise was talking "from fear and not reason".
I do not think I should trespass upon the time of the committee to read the whole of it. However, there are one or two other points.
He charged that continued centralization of taxation by the federal government was leaving the municipalities as "the forgotten people".

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Present tax relations, Mr. Diefenbaker maintained, are a "haphazard outgrowth" of wartime agreements which don't meet the problems of Canada today. The federal government offered "cut and dried" plans-
The difference there is that in the case of this government they were cut and not even dried before the provinces were forced to take them. They were "all wet", and they were "all wet" in more senses than one.
Under a Conservative government, he said, the provinces would have a voice in deciding fiscal terms-
Listen to this!
-the provinces would have a voice in deciding fiscal terms and the tax agreements would contribute to national unity.
Then, at Carman, Manitoba, on May 15, 1957, as reported in the Toronto Star of May 16, we find something very important, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to say something about this one.
No province in Canada will get less tax money from Ottawa if a Conservative government is elected June 10, John Diefenbaker pledged here last night.
The national Conservative leader promised a fair share of tax revenues for all provinces, with more for the poorer provinces but not at the expense of the richer provinces.
This is more of that mirage about which we used to hear, that you could give more services, have lower taxes and still balance the budget. This is one of those myths of the balmy days of 1957 that have gone with the wind.
The larger provincial shares, he indicated, would come from tax money now retained in the federal treasury.
At that time, of course, the Tories were going around saying that Mr. Harris had left the treasury bulging with money. I believe the Minister of Finance has a different line now.
Mr. Diefenbaker made this pledge to almost 700 persons who overflowed-
And so on. Then, at Victoria, on May 21 -I think this, sir, is really a honey, and I hope the Minister of Finance is listening- this statement was made:
"The plight of the municipalities is becoming tragic because there is a constant increase in federal taxes. Now the federal government takes the attitude that there is no responsibility on them to assure that the municipalities shall have the right to discharge their responsibilities-
"The municipalities find themselves unable to carry on because they are being restricted of the sources of revenue."
The premiers of many provinces, he said, had complained there was no recognition of their fiscal needs.
"Even the city of Victoria has to pay outrageous rates of interest today."
This is in 1957, and I should like to know what they pay in 1959.

The time has come for a meeting of the provinces and the federal government, with the municipalities present, to discuss these problems.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Order, I wonder what the idea of the hon. member who has the floor is as to the scope of this debate? He seems to cover the whole realm of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. I am not sure if he is right in doing that. It seems to me that the section continues for one year an increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent of one particular arrangement-that is the allowance, I think it is-with respect to personal income tax as a factor in calculating the tax equalization payments. Is that not it?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: What the bill does in itself is a relatively limited thing.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I wonder whether it is necessary or appropriate to debate the whole concept of the division of revenues between the federal government and the provinces and the municipalities on a bill that is as narrow as that. I should like to have a little bit of guidance on that point.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I might say to Your Honour that I completely agree with you. We are told that this bill is a temporary measure for one year only pending the permanent measure which the present government promised before it was in office, and which it has continued to hold out some hope of extending to the people since. I am seeking to argue that instead of bringing this temporary measure before us for a period of one year only-and the duration of one year is extremely important to my argument-the government and the minister should explain to us why the government did not do what it undertook to do when it obtained a mandate from the people. I suggest that this measure which is brought before us is an entirely different one from the measure for which the government obtained a mandate. In order to make that argument it seems to me I must show what the nature of the mandate was. I have been trying to confine myself strictly within those limits, with this one exception that in making that argument-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Even following the hon.
member's argument in that respect, may I ask whether he should not relate his proposition that the government is not doing something that it promised to do to this narrow field rather than to the broader field. In this bill the government is not saying that this is the only provision with respect to federal-provincial arrangements that it is putting forward.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am seeking to show that that is precisely what it is and indeed that the government has forgotten these other things which it promised to do. It seems to me that it is the proper scope of debate. When the government seeks, as we as an opposition think it does, to mislead the people and to fool the people, it seems to me that it is the proper function of an opposition to bring to light the facts relevant to this measure. The excuse that the minister gave-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I take it that the hon. member is leaving the point of order that was raised.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
No; I am not leaving the point of order. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could possess his soul in patience until I am finished. When the minister introduced the first bill in 1958 he indicated to us that this was an interim measure pending the resumption of the conference which had been promised and that, in succession to that bill early in 1958 in the previous parliament, something else would come. He told us the same thing with less conviction last year. He told us that with still less conviction this year. In other words, what we are being asked to do is to accept this bill.
What seems to me to be the governing point is that this is a one-year measure. I am suggesting that the principle of the bill, in its being a one-year measure, is entirely unacceptable. So that Your Honour may perhaps more readily see what is the trend of my argument, may I say that I intend to show that either the government should come clean and admit it has nothing else to offer and then propose a bill that would extend this until 1962 when the parent act also expires, or, alternatively, they should tell us now what it really has in mind as the successor of this legislation. It seems to me that matter is entirely relevant to the principle of the bill, and I have no intention of departing at all from that line of argument. If the Minister of Finance wishes to say something, he now has the opportunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I should say thank you to the hon. member who permits me now to have a word on the point of order. Apart from other considerations, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that this has now become the third debate in this session on the subject of dominion-provincial relations. It has become that because hon. members in the opposition will not recognize the rules of the house. The first debate on dominion-provincial relations in the present session was held on February 9 and 10 on an amendment introduced by the hon. member for Essex East. It is to be found at page 826 of Hansard and is as follows: 66968-9-215J
Dominion-Provincial Relations
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations."
That amendment, Mr. Speaker, was negatived by the house by a vote on February 10 as recorded at page 885 of Hansard. In that debate we heard the same speech that we are hearing today.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I did not speak in that debate, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: No, not the same speaker. We were denied the inexpressible privilege of listening to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in that debate. But his near neighbour the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) then made the same speech that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is making now. Then we have had speeches on the same subject smuggled at every opportunity into other debates during the session by hon. members opposite. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate smuggled one in within recent days-

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: On a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
-on a matter that was not related to the matter in issue. But there was indulgence shown to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who is always ready to test, try and take advantage of any indulgences. We had this same ground covered again at the resolution stage. Members were not restricted as I urged them that they should be in the light of the fact that the debate had been held on this wide-ranging subject on February 9 and 10. They covered the whole area again. Now the hon. member is back trying to repeat the same thing again.
I recall, Mr. Speaker, that I chided the Leader of the Opposition about introducing that amendment on this subject on a supply motion back on February 9, when he knew very well that we would be bringing in this resolution and bill not long after that and that there would be full opportunity to talk about the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, his answer then was, "This will shorten up the debate when we come to that bill". It has not shortened the debate, Mr. Speaker, because hon. members opposite have blithely disregarded the fact that there was discussion on this matter and they have gone over the whole area again.
With great respect, Mr. Speaker, I submit that this bill is confined to one thing and one thing only. It proposes to amend one section of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act and to do so for one

Dominion-Provincial Relations purpose and one purpose only, namely to raise from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the provincial share of the yield from personal income tax in this present fiscal year. That is what it does and it does no more than that. In my respectful submission this wide-ranging debate, this odyssey into the realm of federal-provincial fiscal relations is quite out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: If this bill is not passed, the effect would be to leave the exemption at 10 per cent, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Not the exemption, Mr. Speaker. The provincial share would then remain at 10 per cent. The one thing the bill does is to raise to 13 per cent for this present fiscal year the provincial share of the yield from personal income tax.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The point on which I wanted assistance was what the minister and the hon. gentleman who had the floor felt was the proper scope of debate. I take it that the minister feels that the debate should be limited to a discussion of the desirability of increasing from 10 per cent to 13 per cent for another year the exemption of tax. Can he say whether that necessarily involves other aspects of the agreement and arrangement between the provinces and the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Not at all. The other provisions of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act continue without change. There is no change made in the agreements which have been entered into between the federal government and the provincial governments in pursuance of the act. All this does is to enable the federal government to pay to the provinces this additional 3 per cent yield from the personal income taxes for the present fiscal year. That is its complete effect, no more, no less.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I have a word on this very point of order. I noticed with great interest the point you raised with reference to what had been said by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), and I had decided to let well enough alone and that nothing needed to be said. However, the minister, who is considered an authority in this house by a goodly number of people, has raised the point which I noted very carefully you had not raised, which was that when the house has made a decision in the same session, the minister's contention seems to be, that subject matter may not again be debated within the same session regardless of the legislation which may be introduced after the decision has been made in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is a position which I would maintain would be completely unacceptable. If we accepted that proposition, all the government would have to do in order to prevent any debate on any of its contentious legislation would be to sit and wait until the opposition had obtained a verdict on an issue and then bring in some very controversial legislation on that very subject. Then the house would, according to the minister's interpretation, be blocked from having a proper debate on the bill in question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: What nonsense.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I think the hon. member's apprehension on that score is not warranted, because the debate on this general field was a debate on the holding of a conference, and that has been disposed of. I would think it quite improper to reopen or redebate that decision today. The debate, of course, on the resolution stage is an inevitable duplication in our system of debating a bill three times, or four times if you count the committee stage, if the house wished to do so. I suppose that is just a precaution against inadvertent or ill-considered legislation. But I think it has been well established that where a section of an act is amended it does not open up the discussion of the whole act. That has been well established and well laid down. The trouble with this subject is that it is so intangible. At least, it has so many ramifications that it is hard to draw the line, but I think the debate ought to be restricted to the proposition which is before the house and criticism of the government for having taken that particular stand.
I admit that that necessarily opens the door to a reference to what else might have been done and what else the government promised, but I think that discussion too ought to be with relation to this particular amendment, which is an allowance of the equivalent of a percentage of income tax. It will take a little time, but this might be a long debate if it were not clear what we were trying to do. I would therefore ask the house to keep as closely to this specific item as it can, because the rules are clear that that is what we are supposed to do when debating an amendment to a specific section.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was hoping to avoid this by pointing out at the outset that I was not going to open up the debate of February 9, and I have not, at any stage, urged or said that I thought there ought to be a federal-provincial conference now or at any other time. I have been keeping completely off that subject. It may prolong my argument a little to have to point out at each stage that increasing Mr. Harris' 10 per cent to the present minister's 13 per cent

is not carrying out what the people of this country were led to believe would be done in this field, and in this specific field, when they elected this present government. It does seem to me that perhaps the Minister of Finance, having used this rubber stamp method of dealing with the provinces, now thinks that this house should also be treated as a rubber stamp, and that all we can debate is whether it should be 14 per cent or 11 per cent, or else we must keep quiet.
What I am saying is that this bill is not what the people were led to expect. In the first place, they were led to expect that this problem was going to be solved, and not that the government were going to be given an annual reprieve, as my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's described it. It seems to me that, we should consider what the Prime Minister said at Victoria on May 21 as to what he intended to do about this problem of federal-provincial fiscal relations. What he said was that the government intended to convene such a meeting in the spirit of confederation. He said that if action was not taken we would find ourselves in a position in five years where the municipalities would be bankrupt or unable to carry out their responsibilities.
I say that this is a very poor substitute for that promise. That was apparently something which was to be done urgently. Two years have already passed almost to the day since the Prime Minister made that statement in Victoria, and we are ask to approve another interim arrangement for another year. It is obvious that nothing more will be done about this urgent problem for one more year, although the Prime Minister had said that in five the direst things would happen, and we have already disposed of three of those five years.
Then the Prime Minister said at Saskatoon on May 27-and I will make these remarks as brief and direct as possible-that no province would receive less than it is receiving under existing fiscal relations. Well, that is true. Then the Prime Minister added that no new fiscal agreement would be made "except by agreement of all". This bill is introduced by agreement with no one except with the majority of this house. It is an enactment of this house and the provinces can take it or leave it. No province agreed to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: But they all take the money.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
They take the money, just as they took the money which Mr. Harris' bill provided in exactly the same way. That was the "take it or leave it" which the minister used to complain about, but all he is
Dominion-Provincial Relations doing today is exactly the same thing except that Mr. Harris discussed the question with the provinces, and Mr. St. Laurent discussed it at five different meetings with the provinces over a long period, and had a great deal of correspondence, before reaching a decision. Mr. Harris did not send a telegram on Saturday saying, "We will be doing this on Monday, and if you do not like it, it's too bad, but that promise made last November to have a conference is no good any longer." That is the difference between what we are asked to do here and what the people were led to believe would be done.
Then at Prince Albert-and this is surely very different from what the minister is doing in his bill-the Prime Minister told his audience that if elected the Conservatives would call a federal-provincial conference at once, with the municipalities invited to sit in, to "distribute the Canadian tax dollar to suit all provinces". This certainly is not doing that. This bill is certainly not doing what we were told would be done right after the election. Another thing which was said at Prince Albert was that one result of the conference would be to ease present tax burdens on Canadian municipalities. I do not think the minister would contend for a minute that he has done that by this bill. At least, if he did, he certainly would not find his friend Mr. Gardiner, the super-mayor of Toronto, agreeing with him, because we know his views. He would not find the premier of Ontario agreeing with him either, and he certainly would not find the premier of Manitoba agreeing with him.
There is other evidence of the same kind, but I do not intend to be repetitive, sir. This is what we were told would be done as compared with what is now being done. The Prime Minister said at Three Rivers on June 4, 1957, according to the Montreal Gazette:
The Conservative party will restore the true meaning of the British North America Act which guarantees the provinces freedom to carry out various spheres of activity allotted them under the constitution.
We will not only make sure that the constitution is respected-we will make sure that the provinces and municipalities have sufficient money to do the job they are supposed to do.
And this is how this is being done!
Having the power to do a certain job does not mean very much if you have not the financial means to implement these powers.
I believe, Mr. Frost is still saying that. So, I believe, is Mr. Duplessis and so, certainly is Mr. Roblin, the premier of Manitoba. And here is the last of these quotations. At Woodstock on June 6, the leader of the Conservative party said:
A Conservative administration would summon a dominion-provincial fiscal conference in the fall to revise the tax structure-
3396	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations
And this is the revision. It was not done at the conference; it was just brought in unilaterally and the provinces could take it or leave it.
That is the record. There were no doubts, no problems, before June 21, 1957. You just called a conference; you all loved one another and the problem was quite easy-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: You are talking about a conference again, and that is out of order.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am not talking about any conference that is going to be held. I am talking about the conference that was held here in Ottawa, the conference out of which the minister claims this bill came. I am talking about the very origin of this bill, and surely not even the minister will claim that that is out of order. He surely will not contend that it is not competent in a debate on the second reading of a bill, to discuss the origin of that bill. The minister told us in January 1958, when he introduced a bill which was exactly the same as the present bill except for the dates, that it was in substitution for the resumption of the conference, which held a two-day meeting in November, 1957. It was to tide them over the period when parliament was meeting. He did not say "until the election was over", because that was a dark secret then. He said "while the session was on", and explained that there was not enough room in this building to accommodate the conference while parliament was sitting, though Mr. St. Laurent did not find any difficulty on that account. When there was a will, there was a way, but when there is no will, no way can be found. The reason we have this bill before us, for a third time, is precisely because of what happened at that conference, precisely because it was the most disillusioning experience that this new government has had, among the many disillusioning experiences it has suffered. Let us see what this conference was supposed to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order. The hon. member is just doing the very thing which, if I correctly understood the view which you expressed earlier, Mr. Speaker, is quite out of order. He is going back now and advancing the most spurious connection between the argument with which he wants to delay the house and the bill itself. There is no such connection as he is trying to maintain, and all these arguments with which he is now seeking to delay the house and the payments to the provinces, are entirely without relevance to the matter before us as I understand it.


Our purpose at this stage, as I conceive it, is to debate the principle of this bill, and the principle of this bill is concerned with raising the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax under this statute. The statute is not opened up to discuss other matter. This bill proposes to amend one single provision of that act. It is quite obvious that the hon. member is just going ahead to make these endless, repetitious remarks in an effort to cover matters which are not relevant to the bill within the rules of this house.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: If I may say a word on the point raised by the minister. I think it comes with singularly ill grace from a minister who read endless documents for three hours in a very recent debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: All relevant.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: -and who also took part in a very celebrated debate in 1956 when he refused to accept the ruling of the Chair and had to leave the chamber-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Is this relevant?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am discussing whether this is relevant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: This demonstrates the irrelevancy.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I listened to the minister patiently and without interruption. Perhaps he could reciprocate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman could stick to the point.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The minister will have an opportunity to speak later, and if he should stray from the point I will not raise points of order.
The principle of this bill, says the minister, is to raise the provinces' share of the personal income tax from 10 per cent to 13 per cent under the federal-provincial taxsharing agreement. Mr. Speaker, the principle of the bill is surely nothing of the kind. That is the modus operandi of the bill. Surely, the principle of the bill is to provide the provinces with a share of the direct taxes. That is the principle of the bill. It is the principle as enunciated by Mr. Walter Harris when the statute which we are now asked to amend was introduced, and it was the principle to which the minister pointed with great satisfaction when he claimed that he was following it in a more generous way only a little over a year ago. The principle of the bill is not merely the arithmetic of the bill but the purpose of the bill, its object, why we are doing it at all. Why do we have this federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangement at all? We have it for many reasons and I am not going to enter into a discussion of

these reasons now, because that would be debating the main measure. We have it primarily in order to divide as equitably as possible the direct taxes in which the federal government and the provinces are entitled to share under the constitution. And I am maintaining that this bill does not do what the government said it was going to do before the Minister of Finance introduced the original bill of which this present measure is the successor.
The minister now says that this measure did not arise out of the conference. If I had Hansard here for January 25, 1958, I think it was-that Saturday morning when the minister said the conference could not be resumed for certain reasons and that, in substitution, he was taking this course-I could prove otherwise. Now he says there is no connection between the two. It seems to me that the minister has answered himself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I have the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act of 1956 here. It contains a great many sections and it deals with a great many different things. I would think that while this bill does, in effect, change the amount of the payment which will be made-the amount of the share which will accrue to the provinces-it does not change any of the principles which were settled by this act passed in 1956. The house then took its decision on the general scheme for a division of revenues between federal and provincial authorities.
All this bill seeks to do is to alter one of the component parts. That does not open the door to debating the question of how corporation taxes or estates taxes are dealt with, or anything of that kind, nor does it open the door to the debating of the negotiation of agreements which have been concluded, except in so far as this legislation may change those agreements. I admit it is not easy to define a narrow pathway, and I certainly do not wish to restrict debate, but I feel that if the whole subject is discussed we would not be following the course that this house should follow.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I was about to read from the opening speech made by the Prime Minister at the conference. I should like to read a sentence or two, and I think Your Honour will see how directly it is related to this particular bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to indicate in what way it is related he should do so.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It is related because it states what the government intends to do in this precise field. I wish to refer to what
Dominion-Provincial Relations the Prime Minister said at page 8 and I shall try to leave out every irrelevant sentence. I hope the minister, in consequence will not accuse me of taking statements out of context. Here are the Prime Minister's words:
We have given our undertaking that when new fiscal arrangements are determined on-
That is to say, new fiscal arrangements with the provinces. I continue:
-no province will receive less than it is now entitled to. But I want to make this clear at the beginning. We are not placing before you any "take it or leave it" attitudes;-
Those words were spoken on November 25, 1957, two months precisely to the day before the take it or leave it attitude was placed before the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I continue.
-we are not taking any hard or fast positions. We are not placing before you any rigid formulae. This conference was convened to seek your ideas and your proposals.
In other words when this conference was held the Prime Minister said that the course this government would follow in federal-provincial fiscal relations was to seek the ideas of the provinces and to get their agreement. But instead of doing that, the government has used its overwhelming majority to impose a particular piece of legislation upon the provinces. That was the point I was seeking to read from this part of the proceedings.
I am sure the Minister of Finance will be able to contain himself while I read something that he himself said on one of the Press Conference programs on which the minister always distinguishes himself to such a marked degree. This conference was held on November 26, 1957. The minister was asked the following question by Mr. Blakely, an old friend of his:
We have just had a new federal-provincial conference, and yet the only one thing which did not emerge from that was a new tax arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is not going to interrupt too frequently on points of order, I can assure him I will not be saying again what I have said in the house on other occasions on the matter now before us. I will not be as long as other speakers have been. I have not any doubt in the world but that all hon. members in the house are going to support the amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing

Arrangements Act as it is offered by the government. However, that is not going to prevent us from underlining, with as heavy a marking pencil as we can, our contention as to the inadequacies of the amendment that is offered at this time.
The present Minister of Finance has by way of the budget seen fit to impose additional tax burdens on the people of Canada to the extent of $352 million for the period of a full calendar year, and yet in the amendment he is offering he is making it very plain that he is not pretending to let the other levels of government receive any of the increased taxes that he is hoping to garner for the federal treasury. We deplore especially the arrangement whereby once again we are being asked to accede to the ten provincial ministers of finance having an assurance as to what their receipts from the federal government may be for only a 12-month period.
We have long contended that the original approach taken on federal-provincial taxsharing arrangements ought to prevail, that is that the minimum time for which an arrangement should be made should be at least five years. As conditions have now existed over a number of years, all we are doing is to assure the provinces of their receipts from Ottawa for the ensuing 12 months. This is hardly good enough in that it completely handicaps the provinces in so far as any long term planning is concerned. We feel that this house has had enough of these annual amendments such as the one now being discussed.
We feel also that the government is certainly less than honest when it presents an amendment of this nature to our Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, while at the same time carrying on negotiations for financial arrangements with certain of the provinces that are not being revealed to the House of Commons. I have particular reference to the announcement of the premier of Ontario indicating very clearly that, in his opinion at least, negotiations are under way for another kind of financial arrangement not yet disclosed to the house. I should like to refer also to the indication on orders of the day yesterday that negotiations are taking place with the province of Manitoba. These negotiations, too, are not covered by the proposed amendment or by any explanation of the need for the proposed amendment. I have reference in particular to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) as recorded at page 3327 of Hansard for May 5, 1959, when he said, referring to Manitoba:
-I may say that no decision has yet been reached.

I feel that if the minister wants to be honest with this house in offering an amendment of this nature he ought, in all fairness, to reveal to this house at this time, and to the people of Ontario and Manitoba, whether or not there are some arrangements being made in the back rooms of the Conservative party about which this house should know. We feel it is an insult to the integrity of parliament to be asking parliament to approve this measure, inadequate as it is, when there may well be other measures of even greater significance in the offing. We feel that if there are other measures in the offing the time to reveal them to the House of Commons is now when we are asked to renew this amendment to the act. I realize very well that Premier Roblin and his supporters are running around the province apologizing for the actions of the Diefenbaker government. I feel that now, not next Wednesday, is the time to reveal the intention of this government.
