As I rise to discuss the principle underlying the bill before us, Bill No. C-41, I feel that possibly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) might not have the same patience with me as we have had with him on certain occasions when he was endeavouring to explain his problems to us. I feel that if he has such problems, and possibly duties to perform, he will be more patient in listening to me present the problems which I feel I must present on behalf of my constituents in the riding of Nickel Belt.
The principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is one which is most important in Canada because it represents an effort to solve a problem which has grown greatly and which represents a burden to every citizen. I refer to the problem of how they can manage the high rate of expansion brought about by our way of life, in addition to the burdens imposed by having three forms of government, federal, provincial and municipal. The workers in my area do not have three salaries, one to assign to the expenses created by the federal government and the other two to provide for the necessary expenditures of the provincial and municipal governments. It is, therefore, in an attempt to solve this problem that the government has introduced the amendment to augment by 3 per cent the provincial share of the revenue for a period of one year.
Apparently this government is interested in this problem only by way of anniversaries. Last year we had this extremely short amendment which we were told was to be for one year. Definitely the people of Canada, if they have followed the discussions in the house, expected that this government was studying the solution which they had

Dominion-Provincial Relations promised of this problem of sharing taxation which necessarily would alleviate the burden caused by the works which are undertaken by our municipalities and works and services undertaken by the provinces. I say that the bill before us today in no way solves this problem.
Moreover, this bill which is before us today indicates that this government has absolutely defaulted in connection with the study which was required of the problem, something which, of course, we all know was discussed at great length by the members of the government prior to the last election and the one preceding it.
In connection with the principle and problem involved in this 3 per cent increase, I should like to quote some of the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) prior to the last election concerning the solution of this problem of tax sharing with the three levels of government. I have a quotation dated June 3, 1957, from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. Here are the remarks attributed to the Prime Minister on that occasion. It states:
A Conservative government will call a federal-provincial fiscal conference at which there "must be municipal representation"-
We see by this bill-

That was the time when it would have been relevant to follow the line of argument which the hon. member is now attempting to follow. However, he cannot do it on this narrow, limited bill which amends one section of the act. I refer him to the ruling made by the Speaker of the house on November 14, 1949, and which appears in the Journals for 1949 at page 237. It reads in part as follows:
On the second reading of an amending bill-
And that is what this is.
- (honourable members will notice that this is an amending bill)-it is the principle of the amending bill, and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration". The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill. If, for example, a bill were introduced to amend a certain section of the Criminal Code of Canada, the discussion would have to relate to the principle of the particular amendment. It would be irregular to enter upon a general discussion of the Criminal Code as a whole.

In order to do that I should like to indicate that because of the knowledge which we have outside the house and the knowledge which we have inside it, this government has not performed those things which should have been performed in order to obtain a better arrangement than the increase to 13 per cent.
With all due respect, may I say this. If we were now discussing an amendment of the Criminal Code, as was mentioned in the

But I think it would be outside of the meaning of the reference-and I say this with all due respect-to state that if we were discussing an amendment of one section of the code we could not discuss meetings or conventions concerning studies of that amendm ent.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am stating now that this amendment concerning the 3 per cent increase for one year only, as I stated before, does not give the provinces the tax sharing possibilities which they were led to believe would be made available. My people in northern Ontario today are more burdened than ever. The costs of services of local governments and provincial governments have risen greatly. My people feel that they have been unjustly treated by this minimal increase which is, after all, a repetition of last year. I am of that opinion, and my people hold it much more strongly. I am sure the Minister of Finance will not disagree with me, having regard to the indication made by him along with his leader that they had absolute solutions to this problem which would bring about the desired result. This government has stated that with respect to this tax sharing problem they would do things which are not even included in this bill. I should like to see them included. I think I am entitled to mention that matter. We have spoken of fiscal relations with the provinces-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The hon. member has indicated that he is going into a discourse which I think is not in order. I think it is quite proper to indicate in general terms that the bill does not go far enough, as the hon. member has already done, or that something else should be done. I have no objection to his doing that, but I would not permit a debate on all the other things that should be done.
Dominion-Provincial Relations

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: But surely, Mr. Speaker, no hon. member should be restricted or prevented from saying that he thinks a bill is totally inadequate having regard to the purposes it is supposed to have or was proclaimed to have. As I apprehended what the hon. gentleman was proposing to do, that was all he had in mind, namely to indicate that these crumbs from the rich man's table-that is what the minister would call it; I will not call it that; I think that was one of the phrases he used when he was over here on this side of the house-would not be adequate.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems obvious that when this government discussed before the Canadian people the solutions which they had, they led them to believe, as far as my province is concerned, that it would receive in the neighbourhood of $100 million last year, and that was stated by the premier of the province from which I come, and stated on many occasions. Undoubtedly this bill does no such thing. That is what I am trying to place before the Minister of Finance and this government the manner in which they led the people to believe they would find a solution to their great problem. I certainly cannot see it in this 3 per cent increase. For instance, it was stated that the municipalities should have some benefit from new fields which would be opened to them, but we did not receive them.
The Prime Minister has stated that Canadian unity would be solved. He stated that a concerted "study"-if you do not wish me to use the word "conference"-of this problem would bring about a complete redress of injustices which they thought existed. This bill will make the people realize that they will only get this very small gift-and I use that word-for another period of one year. They will only get this small increase.
Possibly the Minister of Finance will permit me to indicate to him how different this amendment is compared with a similar amendment which was brought before this house under the previous administration, the Liberal administration under Mr. Harris as minister of finance. We heard a lot last year about the amendment which we are now renewing by way of changing the date of its expiration. We are renewing the same amendment which was before us last year, and it was said then that the province of Ontario would receive by this amendment $22 million. Well, we knew within a year after that that there was no such thing. This government had failed to realize that this percentage increase of income tax was certainly dependent on the prosperity of this country, and therefore because we suffered

Dominion-Provincial Relations under this regime a recession last year in the incomes of our Canadian people, the $22 million which was thought of in the first place turned out to be a mere $18.9 million.
Now what was the increase granted under the Liberal party in 1956? I would like to refer the house to some figures. We have the figures under the previous arrangement before this act which we are now amending came into effect. If we look at the figures under the previous arrangement, the provinces, including Ontario, in all received $156.8 million. That reference will be found by the minister at page 114 of the 195758 budget. If you care to find the figure for the first year under which the Liberal amendment was made, Mr. Speaker, you will find on the estimates that the figure is $196.8 million, which gave a total increase for the province of Ontario of $40 million. This government contends that because the province received less than the $19 million increase by this amendment it has found a complete solution to the problem in which my province, as well as all the other provinces in Canada, found themselves.
We have ways and means of making promises about this bill which we are now studying. We have the outside promises, which I am not going to quote. I would like to, because it would be very good for the memory of the Minister of Finance and members on the government side, when they were about the country electioneering before the last election. But the people in Ontario construed the promises which were made to mean an increase of $100 million to the province of Ontario. Of course, I must realize that we have now classified these promises, and that was one made outside of the house. Then we have the one which I have just discussed a moment ago, as did the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), the one made by way of telegram. Of course, I was not a member of the house at the time, but I understand that there was a slight mistake in the telegram and finally it turned out to be $22 million. But that was a promise which was made in the house, and even that promise made last year on the passing of the bill was found to mean only $18.9 million. That is the type of attitude this government has taken toward its promises, the ones made outside the house as well as the one made inside.
We have been told, Mr. Speaker, that in wanting to solve this great problem of the provinces and our municipalities we would try to satisfy them better by opening the field of possible taxation for them. I realize that this bill does no such thing, but what the government has done is this. While it

has promised new possibilities of money for the provinces and municipalities, instead of giving them more occasions on which to levy possibly their taxation, the government has now raised the personal income tax 3 per cent and the corporation tax three points. In other words, this government is acting in this piece of legislation in the very opposite manner to that promised. It would seem to me that someone should find a way to invent power steering for those people in public office on occasions, because this government is showing by its conduct, and the Minister of Finance who is proposing this bill has shown in his budget speech, that he was prepared to increase taxation and told the provinces and the municipalities-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, surely it is not proper for the hon. gentleman to refer to the budget debate during the course of a debate on the present bill. It is perfectly obvious that hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to talk this bill out today. I think that has been evident all afternoon. They are trying to keep the debate going until their leader is able to return to the house to take part in it some other day.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I would like to remind Your Honour that the other day, when we were debating a supply motion immediately after the budget, the Minister of Finance made allusions to his budget speech. He did not quote from it, but he did make allusions to it. It would seem to me that surely a backbencher would have the same right as the minister.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It is undoubtedly improper to quote from the budget debate because it is obviously just repetition. I did not understand the hon. member to be actually quoting. I think he made a passing reference to something, but he must not quote from the budget debate.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I was making a reference, Mr. Speaker, and I also realize that on one occasion I have had reason to believe that the Minister of Finance was reading at great length from what he called his notes or his files. I have a few important notes which I would like to refer to as well. I would like to indicate that this government has acted in an opposite direction absolutely from that promised in that it has increased its taxes and has sent the provinces and municipalities out to borrow. I notice that the Minister of Finance more or less indicated that that was not the case, and I have here a very good phrase of his in his own speech to which I would like to draw his attention. However, if it is against the rules to quote from his speech, I would simply refer him to page 2415

of Hansard, where he may find reference to remarks of his where he was begging the municipalities to try to borrow to solve their problems. Borrowing has today become very difficult for the provinces-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: On a point of order, surely we are not to have another debate now on interest rates? That subject was fully debated some days ago. The hon. member is just killing time in order to talk this measure out until six o'clock for the purpose which I mentioned earlier and I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, with great respect to ask the hon. member to conform with the rules of the house.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I suggest that the Minister of Finance has made an uncalled for and totally improper reflection on the motives of another hon. member. I did not say that the three-hour marathon of the minister the other day was a means of killing time, and the hon. gentleman has no right to say that the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) is doing so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I accept the hon. member's view that it is not proper to accuse members of ulterior and improper motives. Members are supposed to keep within the rules, and they are entitled to speak as much as they like within that limit.
I must say that this debate has been a hard one to limit because the subject matter is not a definite one and because members have not, I think, been too co-operative in keeping within the narrow limits of this measure. Certainly it is not in order to enter upon a discussion of matters such as interest rates with which we have dealt on a previous occasion.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It seems that the minister and the government do not appreciate at all times that when members of the opposition have occasion to rise-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member proceed with the debate on the bill. It seems there is too much lecturing back and forth across the chamber.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
What I was trying to indicate is that this bill, since it provides the provinces with so little, obliges them, as was suggested by the minister himself, to go out and borrow money, because there is no other way by which they can obtain the extra money which they require. My province is one of those which feel that this 13 per cent is not sufficient, and it will be required to borrow in order to continue the
Dominion-Provincial Relations expansion which is necessary. I feel that this government has defaulted greatly in the light of its promises.
I trust that even now the administration may find the solution which all Canadians have been led to hope would be brought about, and that before too long, as a result of a proper study, our provinces may obtain the money which is definitely needed. It is clear from the complaints which were voiced in this chamber at the time this agreement was announced and on subsequent occasions that it has failed to satisfy the provinces of Canada.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
When I spoke on the resolution stage of this bill I was prevented by the rules from presenting the plea of the municipalities and, particularly, of my own municipality of Gloucester, where education costs have increased 800 per cent in the last 12 years.
This debate has to do with an amendment to the tax-sharing agreement or rather an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. It deals with one point of the formula, and this point was amended in a mild respect last year following a shadow meeting or a cover-up meeting which was held with the provinces. I am trying not to mention the word "conference" because I am sure the Minister of Finance will rise and try to have me ruled out of order.
Today we are again asked to approve an amendment to an interim measure. In other words, this is an amendment to an interim measure pending the convening of a meeting at which special studies may be made of this particular point.
I shall try to show where this amendment does not meet the needs of the provinces and of the municipalities. The 3 per cent increase which was agreed to last year is not sufficient, and it is far from being in accordance with the promises which were made prior to this government taking office. After all, Mr. Speaker, how can principles which were wrong before 1957 be right today just because a different government administers the affairs of the country? When the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act was introduced in this house in July, 1956 here is what the present Minister of Finance had to say as reported at page 6287 of Hansard for July 23:
I point out at the outset, sir, that this is enabling legislation. If it is adopted, it will vest very wide powers in the Minister of Finance, and the power vested in him includes the power to legislate in the form of regulations.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
And then, this has to do with the formula which we are asked to adopt today:
As to the details of the formula, suffice it to say at this point that it is an actuarial maze to most people. The formula itself would undoubtedly confuse most citizens.
And yet today, the Minister of Finance, the same hon. member who was sitting in this house on July 23, 1956 is asking us to approve this same formula with minor amendments. And then the minister continued:
Talk of tax equalization payments, provincial revenue stabilization payments, tax rental agreements, gross national product, average personal income, and other expressions in which this formula bounds make it very difficult for the average citizen to appreciate the niceties of the formula. Indeed, it would be interesting, particularly in the light of the fact that no Liberal member spoke on the resolution-
In this he was wrong, because a few days before two Liberal members had spoken on the very same resolution.
How could the minister blame the government of the day for introducing a formula which he is asking this house to support today? Later on in the course of his speech the minister referred to the municipalities. It has been said in this house time after time that part of this grant to the provinces is intended to relieve the municipalities of the heavy responsibilities, the heavy tax burdens, which they are called upon to bear. Here is what the Minister of Finance had to say about the position of the municipalities as reported at page 6294 of Hansard of April 23, 1956:
The Minister of Finance and the government have been often urged in this house to recognize the fact that the sources of revenue open to the municipalities and to the provinces are inadequate to provide for the expanding cost of education as things stand today. In approaching this present renewal of fiscal arrangements between the dominion and the provinces, the Minister of Finance has a golden opportunity to recognize that inescapable fact and to do something to meet it.
Well, what is he doing today to meet this need of municipalities? He is asking this house to approve a minor amendment to the same act about which he was speaking on July 23, 1956. The explanatory notes of the bill to which we are asked to give second reading today states:
The effect of the proposed amendment will be to extend for a further year the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
The explanation does not refer to one part of the formula but mentions the tax rentals agreements. I feel that the adjustment we are being asked to approve for a period of another year pending the holding of a few provincial elections throughout the country is a far cry from the promises made to the
[Mr. Robichaud.l
electors of Canada during the last federal election campaign. I have in my hand a press clipping dated March 19, 1958, in which the premier of Ontario is reported as having said:
-the $22 million additional tax revenue Ontario has received from the Diefenbaker government, must be regarded as a down payment. Ontario had found it much easier to work with the federal Conservatives than with their predecessors, the Liberals.
The Ottawa Citizen of March 20, 1958, also contains an interesting statement attributed to Mr. Frost:
The premier said the Diefenbaker government was producing "a new deal for the people of Canada" and referred to the October provincial-federal tax meeting as proof.
"After years of getting nothing from Ottawa we came back from that conference with a down payment of $22 million in federal money, which we returned to the municipal taxpayers of this province."

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Yes, down $3 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It is obvious that the premier of Ontario is much easier on the present government and especially on the eve of a provincial election than he was on the former government. Let me quote a statement made by the Prime Minister in Moncton on March 25, 1958, as reported in the Toronto Star on March 26:
The Prime Minister pointed out New Brunswick was getting an extra $2,236,000 annually for the next four years in federal tax-rental grants.
The Minister of Finance introduced early in this session his estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1960, which contain a section entitled, "Special payments to provinces" under which we find:
Payments to provinces as provided under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act (Chap. 29, Statutes of 1956, as amended).
This may be found at page 23 of the blue book. The people of certain maritime provinces were disappointed to learn that the amounts they will receive for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1960 will be much lower than the amounts they received in the previous year. The province of Newfoundland will receive $24,893,000 which is $321,000 less than what was received in the previous fiscal year. The province of Nova Scotia will receive $35,250,000 which is $1,441,000 less than it received in the previous year. The province of New Brunswick will receive $30,266,000 which is $724,000 less than it received in the previous year.
The Atlantic provinces have no guarantee whatever that the amounts they were receiving under federal-provincial grants will be maintained at least at the level they were last year. People in the maritime provinces

who are interested in the affairs of the provinces are today expressing the fear that the special Atlantic grants which are supposed to terminate in 1962 may under this government be terminated simply by an announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) similar to the announcement he made in respect of Newfoundland.
The bill before us today does not meet the requirements of the different provinces and municipalities across Canada. It is no wonder that the Fredericton Gleaner, a newspaper which we know is rather friendly to the present government, in an editorial under date of May 4, 1959 stated:
We have made no secret of our disappointment and regret that the federal government is not giving evidence of its avowed intention of remedying the conditions which plague us in this area of Canada and make us worse off by far than other Canadians.
Pledges were given and the people of the mari-times intend to see that they are carried out. We mean to keep this issue clearly before us.
This is an expression of the popular opinion that exists in the maritime and Atlantic provinces today. It is not surprising that the
Business of the House
people of New Brunswick and other maritime provinces are disillusioned by the actions and attitude of the present government after only two years in office.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock and move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Robichaud the debate was adjourned.
